IF YOU'RE STILL BABYSITTING YOUR AI AGENT, THE PROBLEM ISN'T THE AGENT. IT'S YOU.

Matt Pocock just shipped a 21,000 line feature without hovering over every step.

Then he wrote down exactly how in a 10 page PDF.

His skills repo reportedly has more stars than React.

Here's the formula:

Feature = Codebase + Grill + Spec + Tickets + AFK Loop + Retro

Most people hand the agent the "what" and then micromanage every step of the "how."

He does the opposite.

The 10 layers:

0. Codebase: deep modules and fast feedback. Bad codebases make bad agents.
1. Setup: tell the skills how your repo works, once.
2. Grill: the agent interviews you until every question is answered. Give it the why.
3. Glossary: one word per idea. The reasons go in decision records.
4. Prototype: 3 throwaway versions. Keep the decision, not the code.
5. Spec to tickets: small vertical slices, each one demoable.
6. AFK loop: the agent grabs the next ticket, writes tests first, commits, repeats overnight.
7. Review: a fresh reviewer checks your standards before you even look.
8. Stack and QA: humans only review the decisions you can't undo.
9. Retro: every review comment becomes a lint rule.

The result:

47 user stories.
9 parallel tickets.
About 21,000 lines.
All 12 review comments turned into permanent rules.

Here's my take.

Most developers complaining that AI writes bad code never gave it a good codebase, a clear spec or a single rule.

Then they blame the model.

The agent was never the bottleneck.

The process was.

VIBE CODING DIDN'T CREATE A GENERATION OF BUILDERS. IT CREATED A GENERATION OF STARTERS.

MIT just published the most uncomfortable paper on AI coding.

They tracked every new app on the App Store, Play Store and Chrome Web Store after coding agents showed up.

Devs using autonomous agents wrote 25.5x more code.

Commits up 240%.

Actual releases?

Up 30%.

It gets worse.

After adopting tools like Claude Code, devs wrote 7x more lines and deleted 12.2x more.

Repos abandoned within 30 days went from 60% to 69%.

New apps launching roughly DOUBLED since early 2025.

User engagement didn't move.

Twice as many apps.

Same number of people using them.

I felt this one personally.

I shipped three "projects" last month with Claude Code.

Pretty sure zero humans used any of them.

Here's my take.

AI didn't make people better builders.

It made starting so cheap that finishing stopped meaning anything.

Writing code was never the bottleneck.

Taste was.

Reviewing was.

Building something people actually want was.

And no model is fixing that for you.

THE BEST WAY TO MAKE AI WRITE LIKE YOU ISN'T A PROMPT. IT'S A TINDER APP.

Pasting your old posts into a prompt and saying "write like me" doesn't work.

Here's a way that actually could.

The agent sends you sentences one at a time.
You swipe on them.

"Write in my style" prompts are dead.

You can't describe taste.

You can only show it, one decision at a time.

The people who train their AI like this will sound like themselves.

Everyone else will keep sounding like ChatGPT.

build the tools that make your own process easier to run

completed agent work waits for you

prioritize it. inspect the diff. run the tests. approve what holds up

tokenmaxxing gives you more work to evaluate. what ships still carries your name

MICROSOFT DIDN'T KILL BACKPROPAGATION. THEY DID SOMETHING MORE UNCOMFORTABLE.

They proved we don't always need black boxes.

Researchers had an AI agent, reportedly Claude Opus 5.5, write a neural network's weights by hand.

In Python.

No gradient descent. No training run. No pretrained weights.

The agent writes a hypothesis directly into the weights.

Tests it.

Reads the score.

Rewrites it.

Like a scientist, not a GPU farm.

Then they pointed it at the human brain.

On visual brain scans, it beat every existing interpretable model.

On auditory recordings, it found sound features that predict brain activity.

And on language brain scans, something wild happened.

The score suddenly jumped.

With a black box, that's a paper.

Because this one writes readable code, they looked inside.

The AI was cheating. It was exploiting a flaw in the scan data, not understanding language.

They caught it only because they could read it.

Here's my take.

The AI industry is addicted to bigger.

Bigger models. Bigger clusters. Bigger black boxes.

And nobody can explain what's happening inside any of them.

This paper is a quiet warning.

How many "breakthroughs" out there are just models cheating in ways nobody can see?

virals.name: xsmryze
virals.text:
THIS IS AN ACTUAL F*CKING GOLDMINE

Anthropic just shared one of the best tricks for Claude Code.

The idea: run Sonnet, Haiku 5.5 and Opus 5.5 at once, each one doing only the job it's best at.

Better results and way fewer tokens, because every task lands on the right model.

You just launch Claude Code like this:

claude --model sonnet --advisor opus

here's the split:

→ Sonnet 5.5 runs the session, writes the code and applies the fixes
→ Haiku 5.5 swarms the repo in parallel: search, grep and diff audits
→ Opus 5.5 stays on call as advisor for the big calls and signs off on the diff
→ you stop burning Opus context on work that doesn't need it

Opus only steps in at three moments:

→ before a plan locks
→ when the same error shows up twice
→ before calling it done

Sonnet builds. Haiku swarms. Opus reviews.

JEV engineering is the same move one layer down: the forks that need no thinker (which file, which tool, retry or stop) go to JEV in milliseconds, and the big models only see the ones that split

the full tree
> Sonnet 5.5 runs the main session and coordinates the work
> search maps the repo on Haiku 5.5, read-only
> grep finds call sites on Haiku 5.5 in its own context
> audit checks the diff on Haiku 5.5 in a throwaway worktree
> Opus 5.5 on call as advisor, reviews the synthesized diff before sign-off
> JEV routes micro-forks in milliseconds

paste the tree and this prompt into Claude Code ↓

"Reconfigure my Claude Code setup around this tree:
1. Run the main session on Sonnet 5.5 with Opus 5.5 as advisor.
2. Create three Haiku 5.5 subagents in .claude/agents: search (maps the repo), grep (finds call sites), audit (checks the diff).
3. Set isolation: worktree on audit so its checks never touch my working branch.
4. Add one rule to CLAUDE.md: delegate every repo search and test run to the Haiku 5.5 subagents to keep the main context small.
5. Route fast deterministic forks (tool choice, path selection, retries) through JEV.
Show me every change as a diff first. No edits until I say go."

↳ https://t.co/YqkjQiqRGv

save it, it'll come in handy.

virals.text:
Boris Cherny, Head of Claude Code at Anthropic, just shared an official tip before Fable 5.5 ships

The setup: split your workload across Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Haiku 5.5, and let them talk directly across your open terminals

Zero context pollution between windows: independent sessions ping each other via plain-text IPC over local sockets without burning a single token on conversation history

You just launch Claude Code like this:

claude --model sonnet --settings '{"crossSessionInbound":"accept"}'

here's the split:

→ Opus 5.5 architects session permissions: audits ListAgents discovery, enforces inbound message policies, and signs off on multi-terminal diffs
→ Sonnet 5.5 executes code fixes: builds endpoints, updates schemas, and patches dependent code whenever a peer session reports a breaking change
→ Haiku 5.5 relays inter-session messages: processes SendMessage pings across terminals at 340 tok/s with zero history bloat and sub-millisecond local socket latency
→ you stop burning Opus context on manual copy-pasting between terminals and keep your sessions lean

Opus only steps in at three moments:

→ setting up cross-session topology and inbound security rules before launch
→ evaluating contract diffs when a peer message signals an API schema update
→ signing off on synchronized multi-session PRs before merging to main

Opus architects · Haiku relays · Sonnet executes

JEV engineering is the same move one layer down: the forks that need no thinker (which peer, which tool, forward or drop) go to JEV in milliseconds, and the big models only see the ones that split

the full tree
> Opus 5.5 architects session permissions and audits cross-session topology
> Haiku 5.5 relays SendMessage pings between terminals at 340 tok/s
> Sonnet 5.5 patches code across workspaces when a peer signals a change
> Sessions discover each other automatically via ListAgents and /peers
> Messages travel as isolated plain text over local IPC sockets with 0 context dump
> JEV routes micro-forks in milliseconds

"Rebuild my Claude Code setup around this tree:

4. Restrict all cross-session payload traffic to lightweight plain text via SendMessage with zero history transfer
5. Reserve Opus 5.5 for inter-session capability authorization and final sign-off before committing
Show me every change as a diff first. No edits until I say go"

THIS IS AN ACTUAL F*CKING GOLDMINE

Anthropic just shared one of the best tricks for Claude Code.

The idea: run Sonnet, Haiku 5.5 and Opus 5.5 at once, each one doing only the job it's best at.

Better results and way fewer tokens, because every task lands on the right model.

You just launch Claude Code like this:

claude --model sonnet --advisor opus

here's the split:

→ Sonnet 5.5 runs the session, writes the code and applies the fixes
→ Haiku 5.5 swarms the repo in parallel: search, grep and diff audits
→ Opus 5.5 stays on call as advisor for the big calls and signs off on the diff
→ you stop burning Opus context on work that doesn't need it

Opus only steps in at three moments:

→ before a plan locks
→ when the same error shows up twice
→ before calling it done

Sonnet builds. Haiku swarms. Opus reviews.

JEV engineering is the same move one layer down: the forks that need no thinker (which file, which tool, retry or stop) go to JEV in milliseconds, and the big models only see the ones that split

the full tree
> Sonnet 5.5 runs the main session and coordinates the work
> search maps the repo on Haiku 5.5, read-only
> grep finds call sites on Haiku 5.5 in its own context
> audit checks the diff on Haiku 5.5 in a throwaway worktree
> Opus 5.5 on call as advisor, reviews the synthesized diff before sign-off

outsiders.text:
Boris Cherny, Head of Claude Code at Anthropic, just shared an official tip before Fable 5.5 ships

The setup: split your workload across Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Haiku 5.5, and let them talk directly across your open terminals

Zero context pollution between windows: independent sessions ping each other via plain-text IPC over local sockets without burning a single token on conversation history

You just launch Claude Code like this:

claude --model sonnet --settings '{"crossSessionInbound":"accept"}'

here's the split:

→ Opus 5.5 architects session permissions: audits ListAgents discovery, enforces inbound message policies, and signs off on multi-terminal diffs
→ Sonnet 5.5 executes code fixes: builds endpoints, updates schemas, and patches dependent code whenever a peer session reports a breaking change
→ Haiku 5.5 relays inter-session messages: processes SendMessage pings across terminals at 340 tok/s with zero history bloat and sub-millisecond local socket latency
→ you stop burning Opus context on manual copy-pasting between terminals and keep your sessions lean

Opus only steps in at three moments:

→ setting up cross-session topology and inbound security rules before launch
→ evaluating contract diffs when a peer message signals an API schema update
→ signing off on synchronized multi-session PRs before merging to main

Opus architects · Haiku relays · Sonnet executes

JEV engineering is the same move one layer down: the forks that need no thinker (which peer, which tool, forward or drop) go to JEV in milliseconds, and the big models only see the ones that split

the full tree
> Opus 5.5 architects session permissions and audits cross-session topology
> Haiku 5.5 relays SendMessage pings between terminals at 340 tok/s
> Sonnet 5.5 patches code across workspaces when a peer signals a change
> Sessions discover each other automatically via ListAgents and /peers
> Messages travel as isolated plain text over local IPC sockets with 0 context dump
> JEV routes micro-forks in milliseconds

"Rebuild my Claude Code setup around this tree:
1. Configure cross-session discovery using /peers and set crossSessionInbound to accept

3. Spawn Sonnet 5.5 to execute code edits and synchronize types whenever a peer session reports an update
4. Restrict all cross-session payload traffic to lightweight plain text via SendMessage with zero history transfer
5. Reserve Opus 5.5 for inter-session capability authorization and final sign-off before committing
Show me every change as a diff first. No edits until I say go"

↳ https://t.co/3FlJioxBer
